analysis.one_liner: Shuts down Treasury's federal insurance office and replaces it with a smaller Treasury insurance representative office.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 16, 2026 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has seen no further action; it has 5 Republican cosponsors and no votes.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill eliminates the Federal Insurance Office that Congress created in the 2010 Dodd-Frank law to monitor the insurance industry from inside the Treasury Department. It replaces that office with a smaller 'United States Insurance Representative' focused on international insurance rules, negotiating US agreements with foreign regulators, and deciding when state insurance rules must yield to those agreements. It also swaps the office's seat on the Financial Stability Oversight Council for a state insurance commissioner with a full vote. The bill explicitly leaves state rules on rates, coverage mandates, antitrust, and insurer solvency untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Internationally active insurers and reinsurers, especially foreign-based reinsurers, gain a streamlined process ensuring states cannot enforce rules that treat them worse than US insurers. Treasury gains a leaner insurance operation that uses existing staff. State insurance regulators gain a voting seat on the council that monitors financial-system risk.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the Federal Insurance Office and its director, replacing them with a United States Insurance Representative who handles international prudential insurance policy, covered agreements, and the terrorism insurance program, using existing Treasury resources.

It directs the representative to preempt state insurance measures that disadvantage foreign insurers covered by a US agreement with a foreign regulator, giving internationally active insurers a federal route around less favorable state treatment.

The bill adds a state insurance commissioner as a voting member of the Financial Stability Oversight Council in place of the federal insurance office's role, giving state regulators a stronger voice in systemic-risk oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Insurance consumers lose the dedicated federal office that monitored the insurance industry as a whole and reported on market trends and coverage. State regulators cede some authority over prudential rules affecting foreign insurers to a Treasury appointee, though rules on rates, coverage mandates, antitrust, and solvency are expressly preserved.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurance consumers losing federal market oversight

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the Federal Insurance Office removes the Treasury office created by Dodd-Frank to monitor the insurance industry and gather data across state lines; no other federal office would carry that whole-industry monitoring role.

The bill lets a single Treasury appointee determine that a state insurance rule is inconsistent with a covered agreement and preempt it, with courts reviewing such determinations de novo — shifting real authority over state prudential rules into the executive branch.

Consumer protection under the preemption process depends on the representative's judgment that foreign regulation achieves a level of protection 'substantially equivalent' to state regulation, a standard the representative applies rather than one Congress sets in detail.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The changes are narrow. Giving state regulators a voting seat on the Financial Stability Oversight Council, and explicitly preserving state authority over rates, coverage mandates, antitrust, and insurer solvency, protects important consumer safeguards. But the bill eliminates the only federal office dedicated to monitoring the insurance industry as a whole and moves authority over foreign-insurer rules to a Treasury appointee. The stakes for ordinary consumers are modest; the clearest beneficiaries are internationally active insurers who get a smoother path around unfavorable state treatment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 16, 2026 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no further action and no votes.

narrative.text: Rep. Troy Downing introduced the bill on January 16, 2026, joined by Reps. Fitzgerald and Ogles.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no markup, hearing, or floor action has followed.
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no recorded opposition or support from outside groups in the record so far.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Because the bill is pending in committee, the regulatory status quo — Treasury's Federal Insurance Office and the existing covered-agreement framework — remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Troy Downing
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

for.name: Reps. Fitzgerald, Ogles, and 3 other House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All six initial supporters are Republicans; no opposition has been recorded because the bill has not advanced past committee referral, so the partisan shape of the fight is unknown.

industries.industry: Internationally active insurers and reinsurers (including foreign-based reinsurers)
industries.note: The bill creates a federal process to preempt state prudential rules that treat foreign insurers worse than US ones, and it does this while eliminating the federal office that monitored the industry as a whole. Consumers lose some federal oversight, though state rules on rates, coverage mandates, antitrust, and solvency are expressly preserved, and smoother foreign-reinsurer access can hold down reinsurance costs that feed into premiums.

The bill makes state prudential measures affecting covered foreign insurers preemptible by a Treasury determination, but it also gives a state insurance commissioner a full voting seat on the Financial Stability Oversight Council and requires consultation with state regulators.

industries.industry: Health, long-term care, and crop insurers
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes health insurance, most long-term care insurance, and crop insurance from the new office's scope, leaving their federal and state oversight arrangements untouched.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the House Financial Services Committee since its January 16, 2026 referral with no hearing or markup scheduled. With only 5 cosponsors, no Senate companion mentioned in the record, and no committee action, the most likely path is that it never receives a vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
